tagline: Up a drowned canyon to the Tobacco Plains.
intro: MT 37 leaves downtown Libby and follows the Kootenai River upstream into a narrow, tightly winding canyon, with the railroad on the far bank. Past the east end of Libby Dam it starts to climb and holds to the east shore of Lake Koocanusa, hugging the walls of what used to be the canyon, all the way north to Rexford. Bighorn sheep are often seen on the rock ledges along the way.
The name sounds like a Kootenai word and is not. When the dam was going up, the Corps of Engineers held a contest, and the winner took the first three letters of Kootenai and Canada and added USA.

moments.title: Libby Dam
moments.text: 422 feet of concrete holding back the Kootenai, which backs up 90 miles behind it and some 42 of those in British Columbia.

moments.title: Rexford
moments.text: Rexford incorporated to bargain with the Corps over the dam, and when its old townsite on the Kootenai went under the lake, the town moved up to the new shore.

moments.title: Eureka
moments.text: The road ends here, in country early explorers named the Tobacco Plains after the native tobacco they found the Indians growing, in a town once billed as Christmas Tree Capital of the World.

practical: MT 37 is open year-round. The paved side loop on the west shore, Forest Road 228, is closed in winter.

sources.label: USDA Forest Service, Lake Koocanusa Scenic Byway
